items.titleEn: Snow that may never have fallen
items.bodyEn: Kanbara, the fifteenth post town, was rebuilt on higher ground after a storm tide in 1699. Hiroshige's Kanbara: Night Snow, a hushed village under deep drifts with three bent figures, uses almost no colour and is among the most admired prints of the series. Yet this mild coast rarely sees such snow; the scene is thought to be imagined.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Kanbara: Night Snow (1833–34); Dai Nihon Chimei Jisho (1900–07)

items.bodyEn: Kanbara is written with 蒲, the cattail, and 原, a plain. The same 蒲 hides in futon: the word was first written 蒲団, a round cushion woven from cattail leaves that Zen monks sat on; dan means round. Only later did it mean the bedding you unroll on a cold night, and the spelling shifted to 布団, cloth.
items.sourceNote: Kōjien and Daijirin, entries 蒲団 and 布団

items.bodyEn: 〜と links a condition to what automatically follows: push the button and the door opens, spring comes and snow melts. Because the result must be automatic, the second half can never be a request, command, suggestion or intention. For those, switch to 〜たら: once it gets cold, let's go inside. Where there is a will, と is wrong.
items.ja: {寒|さむ}くなったら、{中|なか}に{入|はい}りましょう。
items.kana: さむくなったら、なかにはいりましょう。

items.titleEn: Even a walking dog gets lucky
items.bodyEn: Inu mo arukeba bō ni ataru: if even a dog goes walking, it bumps into a stick. The first card of the Edo iroha karuta, it cuts both ways. Originally a warning that going out invites trouble, it is now read the other way: get moving and something good turns up. Note the 〜ば conditional of this station.
items.ja: {犬|いぬ}も{歩|ある}けば{棒|ぼう}に{当|あ}たる
items.kana: いぬもあるけばぼうにあたる
